props.title: Gerry
props.initialSlug: Two men lost in desert face dire survival test

sections.content: **Gerry** (2002) represents Gus Van Sant's bold pivot into experimental minimalism. Two men named Gerry (Matt Damon and Casey Affleck) get hopelessly lost while hiking, and that's essentially the entire plot. Van Sant and cinematographer Harris Savides craft mesmerizing long takes of the men traversing stark desert landscapes, letting the camera linger in ways that echo **Béla Tarr**'s meditative style in **Werckmeister Harmonies** (2000). The film's sparse dialogue and emphasis on physical endurance draws parallels to **Walkabout** (1971), though Van Sant strips away even that film's coming-of-age narrative. Walkabout|1971|Two children lost in the Australian outback are helped by an Aboriginal boy on his walkabout|Criterion Last Days|2005|Van Sant's meditation on isolation and fame, loosely based on Kurt Cobain's final days|Prime Elephant|2003|A haunting look at a high school shooting told through tracking shots and overlapping perspectives|HBO Max

Van Sant's "Death Trilogy" of **Gerry**, **Elephant** (2003), and **Last Days** (2005) marked a radical departure from his more mainstream work like **Good Will Hunting** (1997). These films share minimal dialogue, long tracking shots, and an interest in death and isolation. The approach echoes structural films of the 1970s like **Wavelength** (1967), where the camera movement itself becomes the narrative. The trilogy also shows clear influence from Hungarian director Béla Tarr, particularly in their use of extended takes and emphasis on walking as both physical action and metaphor.

The film's sound design is crucial - long stretches of nothing but footsteps and wind create an immersive desert atmosphere that recalls **Meek's Cutoff** (2010) and **Lawrence of Arabia** (1962). But where those films use the desert as backdrop for larger historical narratives, **Gerry** reduces everything to pure existential struggle. The approach influenced later minimalist survival films like **All Is Lost** (2013) and **127 Hours** (2010). Meek's Cutoff|2010|Settlers face harsh survival choices while lost on the Oregon Trail|Criterion All Is Lost|2013|Robert Redford alone at sea with almost no dialogue|Netflix 127 Hours|2010|James Franco trapped in a canyon must make an impossible choice|Hulu SUBHEAD: Impact on Contemporary Cinema

**Gerry**'s radical minimalism helped pave the way for other experimental narrative films like **The Brown Bunny** (2003) and **Paranoid Park** (2007). Its influence can be seen in recent works like **Nomadland** (2020), where landscape becomes a character and traditional plot is secondary to mood and atmosphere. The film's trust in audience patience and visual storytelling also connects to international slow cinema movements, from Thailand's Apichatpong Weerasethakul to Portugal's Pedro Costa.
